extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy and readers of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (commentary/notes)
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly explanatory notes on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, extracting philosophical standards for judging happiness, virtue, moral choice, justice, courage, and related moral concepts. Intended to clarify Aristotle's meanings, distinctions, and illustrative examples for use in study or teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness depends partly on our conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is not a direct gift from Heaven independent of human conduct; supposing it comes at least partly from ourselves does not depreciate its value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If happiness were entirely independent of conduct, motive for self-discipline and moral improvement would vanish. The commentator argues for seeing happiness as partly resultant from our actions and dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of happiness requires whole-life perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Solon's dictum 'Call no man happy till he is dead' implies we should assess happiness with reference to the whole life rather than isolated moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between (a) a man when dead being happy (positive happiness) and (b) the man when dead being said to have been happy; the notes favor evaluating life as a whole rather than momentary states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness should be abiding (enduring)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of happiness in Aristotle's definition is supported by the expectation that happiness should be abiding, based on the most abiding cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This resolves tension between the common idea that happiness is permanent and the empirical fact that fortune changes; the criterion privileges stability/abidingness in the evaluand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goods divided into esse and posse; faculties good only when rightly used
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods either exist in esse (in actuality) or in posse (in potential/ faculties); faculties are good only when rightly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rhetoric is a faculty that may promote justice or be abused to support villainy; evaluate faculties by the moral quality of their use, not merely their existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue requires natural capacity plus action
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature must supply the capacity for virtue, but virtue itself consists in due exercise — one must have the capacity, do the acts, and do them from moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The character of virtue includes the possession of capacity, performance of appropriate actions, and that those actions be done from moral choice (voluntary and deliberate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between moral and intellectual excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are commended merely for having intellectual excellences, but only for exerting and using moral excellences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession of intellectual goods may merit praise without action; moral goods require exertion to be counted as virtues, emphasizing performance over mere possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as regulation of our nature (harmonizing passions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue consists in the due regulation of all the parts of our nature; passions are real parts of nature and should be cultivated into harmony, not extirpated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts Aristotle with Stoics: do not aim at extirpation of passions (pluck blossom off) but cultivate them so that positive enjoyment results (like tuning instruments to produce music).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility lies chiefly in applying rules to particular details
rubrics_metrics.description: It is in the application of general rules to particular practical details that moral responsibility chiefly lies; no rule can be framed to prevent all evasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by citation of Butler; emphasizes the practical judgment required in concrete situations rather than blind rule-following; anti-pattern: assuming perfect rule suffices for every case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habituation law: self-control approaches perfected state by practice
rubrics_metrics.description: By the law of habits the self-controlled approximate a state in which appetites are wholly quelled (perfected self-mastery); conversely, incontinent persons' reasoned remonstrances grow faint until silenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral development is gradual via repeated action; some pain accompanies formation of virtue and only ceases at maturity — a certain degree of pain is necessary to form courage and self-mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturation of virtue indicated by absence of pain
rubrics_metrics.description: No habit of courage or self-mastery can be said to be matured until the pain altogether vanishes; perfected self-mastery results in cessation of the pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a diagnostic: declining pain accompanying previously resisted impulses signals advancing virtue; total absence of pain marks maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action (process) vs fact (result) distinction for moral appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Ilpdii? (action) denotes the whole process from conception to performance; Upa-yfxa (fact) denotes only the result. Moral appraisal depends on action/process rather than merely the resulting fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An outcome may be right though the action/process was wrong (and vice versa). Repetition of right facts without right processes does not form virtue (habit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions form habits and thereby character: evaluate acts by the habit they aim to form
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of each separate act of working accords with the habit they go to form; e.g., separate acts of bravery go to form Courage, hence each such act's object is Courage (honour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate discrete acts in terms of the habit/character they produce over time; anti-pattern: treating single acts in isolation without regard to habituation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral choice requires functioning deliberation, decision, and will
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral choice (voluntary action) involves wish, deliberation, decision, and the will moving the hand; in purely compulsory cases there is only wish, no decision or will, hence no choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To call action voluntary, check whether the will consented following deliberation and decision. Example: throwing goods overboard after decision vs purely compulsory constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good moral choice requires reason to assent when it ought
rubrics_metrics.description: For an action to be a good Moral Choice the Reason must have said 'Aye' when it ought; faults arise if the mental machinery is perfect but wrongly directed, or if the machinery is out of order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish deliberate crime (right machinery, wrong direction) vs akrasia/impairment (right direction from reason but will fails to move).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance affects moral appraisal differently depending on type
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of particular facts affects the rightness not of the irpd^is (principles) but of the vpdylMa (acts); ignorance of principles (incapacity to discern) shows moral constitution to be depraved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess culpability by whether ignorance is factual (reducing blame for particular acts) or principled/constitutive (indicating perversion of conscience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive (veka) and designed causation matter for moral evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: VeKa primarily denotes the relation of cause and effect; from designed causation veKa comes to mean motive or final cause. It would be a contradiction to speak of a man being ignorant of his own motive of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an action, consider intended motive (designed causation) rather than mere accidental outcomes; example: a random shot causing a king's death cannot have had that death as motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: True courage requires accurate danger appraisal and proper motive
rubrics_metrics.description: True Courage requires: 1) exact appreciation of danger, and 2) a proper motive for resisting fear. Spurious forms fail on one or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these two conditions as diagnostic for distinguishing genuine bravery from rashness or foolhardiness; examples: panic due to misleading noise/appearance is not true courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits form through acting under circumstances; one cannot choose circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits being formed by acting in a certain way under certain circumstances, we can only choose how we will act, not the circumstances under which we act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluation should account for constraints of circumstance; formation of virtue requires repeatedly choosing rightly within given situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtue vs confined private vice/virtue (social visibility criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man habitually drunk in private may be viewed as confining his vice to himself and thus law does not touch him; similarly, a religious hermit may confine his virtue to his own person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notes a social/legal distinction: some moral states are deemed private and outside legal intervention; evaluators must distinguish public/social impact from private dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice requires capacity, acts, and moral choice
rubrics_metrics.description: To make up the character of Justice, men must have the capacity, do the acts, and do them from moral choice; all three elements are significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person may act as a 'good citizen' in social duties without being morally perfected; justice as personal virtue demands moral choice, not merely social conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective justice as arithmetic rectification
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrective Justice is wrought out by subtraction from the wrong-doer and addition to the party injured — the rectification is compensatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply corrective justice by restoring parties to prior equality via proportional subtraction/addition; examples and formal proportional reasoning are given (exchange and proportion examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive/particular justice judged by proportional equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Where proportion matters (e.g., dividing profits), fairness depends on maintaining the same ratio between persons as between wares; unequal distribution violates particular justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: dividing profits in ratio 2:3, actual distribution must reflect that proportion; caution before reciprocation ensure same ratio of equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some moral declines are irreversible past a bound
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a point in moral declension at which gravitation operates irretrievably — 'there is a certain bound to imprudence and misbehaviour, which being transgressed, there remains no place for repentance in the natural course of things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a caution: beyond some degree of repeated vice, natural processes make repentance ineffective; relates to Butler's Analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure admitted but to be regulated (Aristotle's middle position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle does not exalt pleasure into the Summum Bonum nor call it wholly evil; he admits its charms but, aware of their dangerousness, resolves to deny himself — 'he feels her sweetness, yet defies her thrall.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pleasures in light of their tendency to harm overall flourishing; neither unconditional endorsement nor absolute rejection is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of moral acts must consider proportionality of social forms
rubrics_metrics.description: In a pure democracy men are numerically equal, in other forms only proportionately equal; thus justice and equality assessments depend on political form and proportional concept of equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating civic justice or rights, take into account the form of government and whether equality is numerical or proportional; the same act may be judged differently in different regimes.
